To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rear surface temperature of an ablative foil rises rapidly at the beginning of laser irradiation, and that the rise is due to the energy transport mechanisms of radiation and electron heat conduction.

the rear surface temperature of an ablatively accelerated foil is dominated by the thermal conductivity of the foil material, and the laser energy absorbed by the foil is not a significant contributor to the heating.
the ablation temperature is 1.3 times the critical temperature for the onset of vaporization and that the preheat temperature for a 10 ns laser pulse is 2.2 times the critical temperature.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that the ablatively accelerated foil is a very useful tool for studying the energy transport mechanisms in a laser-heated target, and that the preheat problem is not nearly as serious as it was once thought.

the ablatively accelerated planar foils have provided a unique opportunity for the study of the physics of high temperature hydrodynamics, radiation and conduction in the presence of strong shock waves.

The main takeaway from our work is that
preheat is a very small fraction of the energy required for fusion.
the laser energy absorbed in the target is efficiently converted to kinetic energy of the target, with minimal heating of the fuel.
the preheating of laser- accelerated targets is minimal at low intensities, and can be controlled by proper choice of laser parameters and target design.
